entry.evidence: This paper focuses on the value and use of daily ozone maps from Level 3, based on a gridding of its zonal coefficients.

sequences.source_document: Published paper (XML text with PDF for figures)

steps.action: Relied on the LIMS V6 Level 2 retrieval and the sequential-estimation Level 3 zonal Fourier coefficient product, both characterized and archived in the authors' earlier work.
steps.quote: The LIMS (Level 2) profiles were retrieved with an improved Version 6 (V6) algorithm.

steps.action: Set the aim of exploring larger-scale variations of Arctic ozone, temperature and GPH in the daily maps without resort to a model.
steps.quote: This paper further explores several instances of those larger-scale variations of Arctic ozone, temperature, and GPH.

steps.action: Produced January 1979 zonal-mean cross sections of nighttime V6 ozone and temperature and the zonal standard deviation of ozone (Figs. 1–3).
steps.quote: Figure 1 shows the latitude–pressure cross section for January from just the descending (D) orbital profiles

steps.action: Compared the zonal means with Smith et al. (2018), López-Puertas et al. (2018), Marsh et al. (2001) and the Fleming et al. (1990) climatology, and flagged an unexpected ozone feature near 45° S.
steps.quote: the rather large ozone values in the upper mesosphere at about 45 ∘ S are not found in other datasets

steps.action: Compared V6 ozone profiles with the nighttime rocket chemiluminescent ozone sounding at White Sands on 15 December; LIMS ozone was larger in the upper stratosphere.
steps.quote: LIMS ozone is larger than rocket ozone through the upper stratosphere.

steps.action: Attributed the mismatch to an ozone maximum along the LIMS view path seen in the 4.6 hPa map, and to space-time variability, rather than to a retrieval error.
steps.quote: There is an ozone maximum along the LIMS view path just to the south of White Sands, which may account for the profile differences.

steps.action: Checked the retrieval premise by comparing V6 temperature with the rocket datasonde; agreement was very good in the upper stratosphere, and co-location effects at 0.68 hPa were discussed.
steps.quote: Agreement between them is very good throughout the upper stratosphere

steps.action: Used the Poker Flat rocket soundings of 27 and 28 January, which happened to coincide with a wave-1 stratospheric warming.
steps.quote: The two comparisons above Poker Flat, AK, occurred at the time of a stratospheric, zonal wave 1 warming event.

steps.action: Compared V6 ozone profiles with the Poker Flat rocket ozone of 27 January, finding good structural agreement into the mesosphere; 28 January was reported as similar.
steps.quote: there is good agreement of the structure between them, even in the mesosphere

steps.action: Identified a low-ozone pocket from 7 to 2 hPa in both the rocket and V6 profiles, plus an unexpected rocket maximum at 0.6 hPa.
steps.quote: The ozone profiles in Fig. 6a indicate the relative minimum in a low-ozone pocket (LOP) that extends from about 7 to 2 hPa.

steps.action: Compared V6 temperature with the Poker Flat datasonde; a 5 K bias implied an ozone bias of -40 % that the ozone comparison does not show.
steps.quote: ought to lead to a V6 minus rocket ozone bias of - 40 %

steps.action: Explained the temperature mismatch as a spatial mismatch: the LIMS view crossed a warmer region (Fig. 7b). The small ozone differences were taken as supporting this.
steps.quote: it is likely that there is a spatial mismatch for V6 and datasonde T ( p ) values

steps.action: Mapped GPH, temperature and ozone at 4.6 hPa and 0.46 hPa on 27 January, placing the rocket site in the Aleutian anticyclone and LOP, with mesospheric cooling above (Fig. S1).
steps.quote: the rocket profile above Poker Flat, AK, was near the center of the anticyclone and in the region of relatively low ozone (or LOP)

steps.action: Concluded that daily Level 3 maps are useful for interpreting ozone fields under dynamically disturbed conditions.
steps.quote: Figs. 4 through 7 and S1 indicate the utility of daily maps from LIMS for analyses of the ozone fields during dynamically disturbed conditions

steps.action: Followed weekly 4.6 hPa GPH and ozone maps from 3 to 17 February (Figs. 8–9) and H2O at 6.8 and 10 hPa; the LOP deepened and then filled.
steps.quote: there was a deepening of the LOP from 27 January to 3 February and a filling of it thereafter

steps.action: Asked whether chemical ozone loss contributed to the LOP between 27 January and 3 February.
steps.quote: [...] chemical loss of ozone from 27 January to 3 February in the region of the LOP?

steps.action: Took candidate mechanisms from the literature: NOx catalytic loss, reduced production at high solar zenith angle, and no enhancement from energetic particle precipitation (Holt et al., 2012).
steps.quote: [...] . (1998) and Nair et al. (1998) conducted model calculations to show how that could happen.

steps.action: Mapped nighttime NO2 and HNO3 at 4.6 hPa on 27 January (Fig. 10), tracing NO2 advection about the vortex and anticyclone.
steps.quote: one can trace the horizontal advection of high NO 2 toward higher latitudes and toward the polar vortex

steps.action: Ran a back trajectory from the LOP and a forward photochemical calculation initialized with LIMS O3, NO2 and HNO3, giving ozone decline from NOx catalytic loss with minimal production.
steps.quote: Results of a time-dependent photochemical calculation conducted along this trajectory in the forward direction are shown in Fig. 12

steps.action: Kept the interpretation that the LOP formed from the interplay of transport and photochemistry.
steps.quote: The LOP formation is a result of the interplay between transport and photochemistry in the high-latitude upper stratosphere in the winter.

steps.action: Mapped the tertiary ozone maximum and temperature at 0.022 hPa on several dates (Figs. 13, S2, S3) and built weekly time series of peak ozone and its latitude (Fig. 14).
steps.quote: Figure 14 shows time series of peak zonal mean ozone at 0.022 hPa and its latitude location for each week from November through mid-March.

steps.action: Compared the peak values and their winter evolution with López-Puertas et al. (2018) and Smith et al. (2018); the V6 increase into February disagrees with Smith et al.
steps.quote: The increase in V6 ozone during winter in Fig. 14 disagrees with that of Smith et al. (2018), who found decreasing ozone by February.

steps.action: Proposed that the February 1979 enhancement responds to wave-driven disturbances following the minor SSWs; this was not tested.
steps.quote: The enhanced V6 ozone of February 1979 follows those SSW events

steps.action: Compared a V6 10 hPa ozone map with the V5 map of Leovy et al. (1985) (Fig. S4); V6 shows sharper gradients, attributed to the shorter SE memory.
steps.quote: The ozone gradients are more pronounced with V6 than with V5 at both the subtropical and vortex edges of the ozone field.

steps.action: Mapped 68 hPa ozone on 15 December (Fig. 15) to examine the tropical SD excess, and found an unexpected high value over the western Pacific.
steps.quote: there is also an unexpected, high value of 2 to 3 ppmv at about 15 ∘ N, 150 ∘ E

steps.action: Checked the feature against the 46 hPa map and against HNO3 and H2O maps at 68 hPa, which show little or no anomaly.
steps.quote: The adjacent map of ozone at 46 hPa appears unperturbed in that region (not shown)

steps.action: Excluded a real ozone feature at 68 hPa in favour of residual subvisible cirrus radiance effects, and cautioned users.
steps.quote: It is very likely that the anomalous ozone at 68 hPa is a result of residual effects from subvisible cirrus

steps.action: Returned to the 45° S anomaly using 0.032 hPa temperature and ozone maps (Fig. S5) and the ascending-orbit views, which show no anomaly.
steps.quote: Ozone mixing ratio anomalies are not apparent along the ascending orbital segment

steps.action: Judged the 45° S upper-mesosphere ozone enhancement an artifact of unweighted tangent-path temperature gradients in the V6 mesospheric radiance calculation.
steps.quote: we judge that it is very likely that the enhanced ozone mixing ratios near 45 ∘ S in Fig. 1 are an artifact

steps.action: Concluded that the Level 3 product, with its noted spurious features, is a resource for interpreting and validating V6 profiles and studying Arctic transport and chemistry.
steps.quote: we pointed out how an examination of changes in their nearby fields is valuable for the interpretation and validation of V6 profiles

Partly: rocket comparisons agree within errors; mismatches attributed post hoc to sampling
Level 3 maps useful with flagged artifacts; LOP from transport plus NOx chemistry

end.claim: The LIMS V6 Level 3 daily maps are a usable resource for Arctic winter ozone, temperature and GPH studies. They aid interpretation and validation of V6 profiles against local rocket soundings, with spurious ozone flagged at 68 hPa in the tropics and near 45° S in the upper mesosphere.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the comparisons of V6 ozone and temperature profiles with the rocket chemiluminescent and datasonde soundings, read against the daily maps, the claim that the maps aid profile interpretation would not exist.

gates.evidence: The LIMS data and rocket soundings were collected in 1978–79, independent of the paper's questions. The rocket comparisons could have failed, but each mismatch (§3 ¶2, §3 ¶5) was explained post hoc by view-path sampling. Nothing was fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Sequential-estimation (Kalman-type) algorithm producing daily zonal Fourier coefficients
Non-local thermodynamic equilibrium effects on ozone and CO2 emission

limits: Headline status: capability_characterized. Sub-claims at other statuses: (1) LOP formation from transport plus NOx photochemistry is best_explanation; the trajectory model output is not compared quantitatively with the observed LIMS ozone change (§4 ¶5). (2) The February tertiary-maximum enhancement as a response to SSW wave activity is an untested hypothesis ('perhaps', §5 ¶2, §7 ¶3); status none. (3) The 68 hPa and 45° S features are judged artifacts as best_explanation by reasoning and indirect cross-checks (§6 ¶3–¶4). Process limits: rocket-profile mismatches are explained after the fact by spatial sampling, without a quantitative test (inference). The evidence covers a single winter and three soundings. The paper makes no explicit novelty claims. The AMT open discussion and reviews (two referees per the review statement) were not supplied, so no review sequence is coded. Several analyses are 'not shown' (0.68 hPa maps, 4.6 hPa H2O, 46 hPa ozone, mesospheric GPH vortex).

disagreements.target: Smith et al. (2018), wintertime tertiary ozone maximum evolution
disagreements.support: The V6 weekly peak ozone at 0.022 hPa increases into February 1979, which the authors attribute to that winter's minor SSWs rather than to an error in Smith et al.
disagreements.quote: The increase in V6 ozone during winter in Fig. 14 disagrees with that of Smith et al. (2018), who found decreasing ozone by February.

disagreements.target: Smith et al. (2018, their Fig. 4), location and magnitude of the NH tertiary maximum
disagreements.support: The January V6 nighttime zonal mean puts the maximum somewhat higher and larger than recent satellite datasets.
disagreements.quote: the NH maximum are somewhat higher and larger than those reported by Smith et al. (2018, their Fig. 4)

disagreements.target: López-Puertas et al. (2018, their Fig. 15), MIPAS mesospheric ozone
disagreements.support: The peak V6 values exceed MIPAS values; the authors suggest V6 temperature or ozone biases as the cause.
disagreements.quote: Those maximum V6 values are larger than reported by López-Puertas et al. (2018, their Fig. 15), perhaps due to biases

disagreements.target: LIMS V5 ozone maps of Leovy et al. (1985)
disagreements.support: The side-by-side 10 hPa maps (Fig. S4) show sharper V6 gradients, attributed to the halved SE memory.
disagreements.quote: The ozone gradients are more pronounced with V6 than with V5 at both the subtropical and vortex edges of the ozone field.

alternatives_considered.chosen: Show the 27 January Poker Flat comparison only
alternatives_considered.reason: Comparisons for the two days are similar

alternatives_considered.chosen: V6 H2O at 6.8 and 10 hPa as a tracer of transport into the LOP
alternatives_considered.reason: V6 H2O fields are noisy at 4.6 hPa

alternatives_considered.chosen: Both combined (A+D) and nighttime-only peak ozone series, nighttime based on zonal mean plus waves 1 and 2
alternatives_considered.reason: Not all profiles reach the 0.022 hPa level
V6 SE memory is half that of V5, so maps are more representative of rapidly changing fields
